body_markdown:
*Ian* writes:


Hi Sajeev, I purchased a 2002 Corvette 21 years ago. It was purchased from a very qualified Corvette sales/repair shop in Tampa, Florida. I purchased the car with a rebuilt title. It had been hit in the back and totaled the year before.


I have put a little over 100,000 miles on it so far. The car has been fantastic and except for normal wear and tear items, has run great. The car is garage kept and still looks great. My question is how would I determine a fair value if I decide to finally sell it?


*Sajeev* answers:


This is a fantastic question, because a C5 Corvette coupe (I am assuming it isn’t a Z06 or convertible) lives in a classic car purgatory where it isn’t old, rare, or “popular” enough to be universally appreciated like a C2 or C3. This means you run the risk (as it were) of pricing your C5 to a retail used car buyer, but I believe you are seeking a specialty or classic car buyer. *Let me explain…*


In my 10-year tenure with a major dealership group, my store managers emailed me (i.e. the guy who liked old cars) when a vintage car showed up on trade. The result was always a low-ball offer, because we didn’t exist to recondition and “sit on” old cars like the specialty dealerships. We genuinely didn’t want 20-plus-year-old cars, as they were often hard to finance with our banks and rarely sold quickly.


These new car dealerships value a 20-year-old specialty car like any other trade-in that will be sold at auction, or to another dealer. That’s understandable considering their business model, but many retail folks use **their** trade-in valuation tools to make an offer on **your** C5.


And that’s the big problem here!


I never let them value my Lincoln Mark VIII, by the way.


[Sajeev Mehta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/sajeev-mehta/)


One such valuation tool is Kelley Blue Book (KBB), but there are plenty of used-car data aggregators available online these days. Their service is both valid and necessary, but a C5 isn’t a C8 or a late-model Toyota Camry. Here’s what KBB pulled up for a trade-in value for a C5 similar to your mileage:


- #3 Good Condition: $7580–$9730
- #2 Very Good Condition (most common): $8030–$10,230
- #1 Excellent Condition (very hard to find): $8380–$10,680


If you are miffed at KBB’s #1 values, join the club. But very few cars are #1 condition, as most vehicles generally need basic maintenance, new tires/brakes, and some cosmetic work (driver’s side seat leather, stone chips, etc). And your C5 is not a #1 car, because of the rebuilt title and the higher mileage.


- #3 Good Condition: $13,433–$20,967
- #2 Excellent Condition: $25,633–$32,467
- #1 Concours Condition: $34,633–$38,967


The data above is what you *should* use, available on Hagerty’s own[Valuation Website](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools) . Clearly, I have a bias for my employer, but I was a user before I got this gig: Hagerty helped my former employer determine what an older car might sell for after modest reconditioning (detailing, basic maintenance, new tires/battery, etc) while KBB helped us with the trade-in offer.


Just like KBB, we classic car enthusiasts rarely find vehicles in #1 (concours) condition, because extremely low mileage and an[NCRS certification](https://www.ncrs.org/shop/index.php?main_page=index&cPath=78_1_80&srsltid=AU7gw4WKJMBfzsoYFQx8Q0dYX341q9QW3fktnntK73MzjNBoV7Go7FCH) are mandatory for most Corvettes. I reckon there are too many low-mileage, clean-title #2 condition C5s for sale at any given moment, so you will likely price yours as a #3 car *.*


Hagerty Valuation Tool


Hagerty also shows trends, and unfortunately the C5 has been losing value over the past five years. But a median value in July 2026 is a little over $16,000, and that’s a fair asking price for your C5, if you have the following:


- New tires from a famous brand name
- A binder full of service receipts
- Paint correction to make the bodywork shine like a #1 condition example
- Fun options, like the F45 adjustable suspension and Heads Up display in working condition
- Original keys, floor mats, owner’s manual, sales brochure, radio, etc.
- Rare options like magnesium wheels
- A generally desirable or rare color, like[Millennium Yellow](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/insider-insight-does-paint-color-really-impact-value/#:~:text=The%20winner%3F%20Yellow.%20Porsches%20painted%20that%20color%20tended%20to%20sell%20for%20nearly%20%243000%20more%20than%20average.%20There%E2%80%99s%20a%20caveat%2C%20though%3A%20Yellow%20Porsches%20also%20seem%20harder%20to%20sell%20than%20other%20colors%2C%20with%20a%20sell%2Dthrough%20rate%20of%2063.6%20percent%2C%20compared%20to%20an%20average%20of%2070.8%20percent.)


The rebuilt title is less of a concern in the year 2026, but only if you refuse offers based on KBB or a similar valuation tool. So I will go out on a limb and suggest that your Corvette can sell for $15,000 to the right buyer. (That’s about five grand more than your average offer made using KBB trade-in data as proof.)


Patience is the key, as the first people interested will always lowball. But if you can honestly tell someone you have perfect leather seats, new Michelin tires, and a paint-corrected Millennium Yellow body, odds are you will make a sale at that $15,000 price.


Good luck in your future valuation efforts, and thank you for this question. Now it’s time to see what our readers think in the comments below!
